prize_parts.citation: For showing, with credible local labour-market evidence, how import competition and technological change reshape employment, earnings and adjustment.

statement.case_for: I keep B036 first, but I have changed the configuration. In round 1 I proposed Autor, Hanson and Katz and defined the discovery broadly, as the skill-premium and task framework plus the China-shock evidence. The exchange showed that this definition is the weakest part of my case. Several colleagues (Boppart, Dreber, Hjalmarsson, Strömberg) objected that it bundles two strands with different authorship, and that Dorn's omission would be hard to defend. I now define the discovery by what the evidence identifies. Autor, Dorn and Hanson show, with local-labour-market designs, how exposure to import competition and routine-task technology changes employment, earnings, migration and adjustment costs. That is a well-defined causal object. The evidence has been replicated, extended and challenged for more than a decade. It changed how economists and policymakers think about the distributional costs of trade and technology, and it showed that adjustment is slow and uneven, which the earlier representative-worker view did not. A three-name set that matches the core papers makes the credit boundary clearer than the Katz version did. The cost is that Katz's skill-premium work, which supplies the longer conceptual history, is not credited. I regard that as a real cost, not a technicality. My chair-summary answer to whether this is one discovery or two is that it can be one if the citation is limited to local-labour-market evidence on trade and technology exposure. It is two if the citation claims the whole task and skill-premium framework. I now take the narrower reading.
statement.case_against: The narrower citation under-credits the task and skill-premium lineage, including Katz and contributors outside the credited names such as Acemoglu and Restrepo. The size, persistence and external validity of the trade-shock estimates are still contested. Shift-share exposure designs have been debated on inference and identification. The evidence identifies local effects, not aggregate welfare effects, so the citation must not claim more than that. If the committee wants a single discovery with a unique credit set, B038 comes closer to that standard, because its credit concentrates in two names. B015 has the larger footprint on policy practice. My field is adjacent to this candidate, and I may be drawn to design-based evidence because of it.

responses.point: Friberg separates confirmation of a mechanism from confirmation of magnitudes. For B038 the selection and reallocation mechanism is better confirmed than the welfare numbers. For B015 the persistence of a workhorse framework through 2008 and 2021-23 shows usefulness and adaptability, and it is weaker evidence that the specific credited building blocks were confirmed.
responses.response: I accept this distinction and apply it to my own candidate. For B036 the identified object is local employment, earnings and migration responses, and that is what the citation should claim. Aggregate welfare effects are not identified, and the debate over persistence means I should not rest the case on any single estimate. This also argues for the narrower Autor-Dorn-Hanson set. His own B036 proposal in round 1 used the same three names, and I now agree with it. The same standard applies to B038. Its mechanism is well supported, but the quantified gains depend on elasticity assumptions, so I would want the B038 citation limited to the mechanism, as he proposes.

responses.point: Boppart agrees on B036's influence and evidence quality. He argues that it is harder to construct as one discovery than B038 because the task and China-shock strands have different authorship. He says the task framework overlaps with prizes already awarded, that choosing among Katz, Dorn and Hanson is difficult, and that the magnitudes remain contested. He sees B038 as a single discovery with a clean credit set.
responses.response: The construction point moved me, and it is the main reason I changed names. Tying the set to the local-labour-market papers reduces the Katz-versus-Dorn dilemma, because those papers define the discovery. I would qualify the overlap point, working from my general knowledge. The 2023 prize concerned women's labour-market outcomes over time. The 2024 prize concerned how institutions form and affect prosperity. Any overlap is in the task-model lineage and not in the cited subject, and the narrower citation reduces it further. I do not claim B038 is weaker on attribution. It is cleaner, and I list it as my first alternative. What keeps me on B036 is that its identified object is more tightly bounded and has been tested harder against its critics. I say that with the caveat that my own field is adjacent to B036.

responses.point: Hassler, as chair, rates B015 strongest on durability and consequence for practice. He sees Calvo and Taylor as the origin of the key building blocks and Woodford as the synthesis. He treats the post-2021 inflation and heterogeneous-agent models as extensions and partial challenges, not refutations. He accepts that omitting Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a real cost.
responses.response: I do not dispute B015's influence or maturity, and it stays on my alternatives. My difficulty is the standard of evidence. Friberg's point that micro evidence on time-dependent versus state-dependent pricing is mixed bears directly on a citation that credits Calvo pricing. The chair's round-1 question on what would confirm or disconfirm Calvo pricing and the Taylor rule as distinct from the framework has not been answered, as far as I can see. I would need either a citation worded around policy rules and the theory of nominal rigidity, as Hjalmarsson suggests, or a clear account of the evidence. The estimation phase would remain outside any three-name set. I would not oppose B015 on grounds of merit. I disclose below that I overlapped with the IIES macro group at Stockholm, and I treat his argument as evidence to weigh and not as a tie to resolve.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B050 first and B036 second. She weights quasi-experimental evidence heavily. She says the magnitude and persistence of the China-shock estimates are debated, that the task framework draws on contributors outside the credited names, and that Dorn's omission would be hard to defend.
responses.response: Her objection to Dorn's omission is one I have accepted, and the new set includes him. I accept that persistence and magnitude remain open, and I would limit the citation to the identified local effects. I also agree with her wish for evidence that targets a specific channel. The China-shock designs identify local exposure effects, not a full welfare account. I take her point that B036 is not clearly ahead of B050 on attribution. I still hold B036 higher, because the empirical record for B050's collateral channel is, by her own description and Strömberg's, mixed. Her view and mine rest on the same standard applied to different candidates.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B036 as an alternative below B015. She argues that B036 bundles two strands with different authorship, that Dorn is left out despite co-authoring the key papers, and that the Acemoglu overlap is a further reason for her to rank it lower. She says B015's difficulty is dispersion within one framework and not a bundle of two.
responses.response: The narrower set responds to the Dorn and bundling points. It does not remove them entirely. A citation limited to local-labour-market evidence leaves out the longer skill-premium lineage, so some bundling risk remains in how the committee describes it. I agree that B015's attribution problem is a different kind: eight names within one programme, not two strands. Neither is cleaner in an absolute sense. I weigh a bounded credit set with a contested magnitude somewhat above a diffuse credit set with a contested empirical standing. I accept that this ordering rests on judgement.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a narrower citation limited to local-labour-market evidence, or insists on the broader task and skill-premium framework, in which case Katz belongs in the set and the choice among the names becomes harder again.
How far the China-shock estimates of local effects generalise across countries and periods, and how much their persistence depends on design and inference choices.
How much credit for task-based models belongs to contributors outside the credited names, and whether the narrower citation avoids that problem or only hides it.

Whether the committee judges the 2021 recognition of natural-experiment methods in labour economics to reduce the marginal case for another labour-evidence prize. I regard the substantive questions as distinct.

Whether B038, with its cleaner two-name set and mature microdata record, is the better choice if attribution clarity is weighted above the identification quality of the evidence, and whether B015 should outrank both if breadth of policy influence is weighted above attribution.

I apply a common standard of direct evidence, but the committee has not agreed one. My assessments rest on general knowledge and the supplied round-1 materials, and I have not independently verified the scientific record or any credit claim.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson or Katz appears in my supplied profile. My field of empirical labour economics is adjacent to B036, and I may favour design-based labour evidence. I also presented the 2021 prize on natural experiments as chair, which may predispose me to that style of work, so I have tried to apply the same criteria to other fields. For other disclosures from my profile: I overlapped at Stockholm University (2010-17) with the IIES macro group, including Hassler and Krusell, who prefer B015. That is an institutional overlap and not a co-authorship. B015 is only an alternative for me. My co-authors, including Oosterbeek, van Ours, Holmlund, Edin, Åslund, Öckert, Johansson and Nybom, do not appear among the credited names on any shortlisted ballot. I have not adjudicated these ties.
